preamble: Retroflexion and fortition of the coda tap [ɾ] to an unreleased voiced retroflex stop [ɖ˺] before /d/, /t/, /n/ or /tʃ/. In western Cuban Spanish, coda /ɾ/ and coda /l/ merge and assimilate to the next consonant. In Havana a sociolinguistic variant of this assimilation is retroflex: when the next consonant is /s/, /d/, /t/, /n/ or /r/, the whole sequence is articulated as retroflex, [ɽʂ], [ɖ˺ɖ], [ɖ˺ʈ], [ɖ˺ɳ], [ɖ˺ɽɽ] (Guitart 1978, 2004; Choy López 1988; as summarized by Arias 2019). So arde is pronounced a[ɖ˺ɖ]e and horno ho[ɖ˺ɳ]o, where the variety without retroflexion has [nn]. Before /tʃ/ only the first element is retroflex (corcho co[ɖ˺ʧ]o), which Arias calls a dissimilation from the non-retroflex [ʧ]. Arias stresses that the retroflexion itself is not an assimilation: "la retroflexión no es un caso de asimilación, ya que se da de modo simultaneo en ambas partes de la secuencia". There is no retroflexion when the next consonant is a dental stop followed by a rhotic (mata[d˺d]ragones 'matar dragones'). Before /s/ the tap stays a liquid, [ɽʂ] (filed under ɾ > ɽ). Word-finally Arias also reports a retroflex [ɖ] alongside [d]; for this position Dohotaru's variationist studies of Havana speech find postalveolar realizations alternating with alveolar ones. Guitart writes that in pre-revolutionary Cuba the retroflex pronunciation was socially unmarked and its absence marked a speaker as of low status; Arias describes the retroflex variety as the more prestigious one in Havana. In the city of Pinar del Río, the acoustic studies of Darias Concepción, which do not detail phonetic contexts, give examples of postalveolar stops in other contexts, alternating with other realizations.
